title: A tiny display, a timer, and a web page on the device

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What if a seven-segment display, the kind on an old clock, had its own web page? That's ESP32-7SEG, a small firmware project by Antoine.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A web server on the clock itself?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Basically. The firmware runs on an ESP32 FireBeetle board and drives an Adafruit seven-segment display over I2C. It also serves a local web interface, so you control the display from a browser on the same network.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What can you do from that page?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's a Timer Control panel. You pick stopwatch or countdown mode. There are quick presets for ten, five and one minute, or you can type minutes and seconds yourself and press start. And there's a button to reset the WiFi, which clears the stored credentials so you can set the device up again.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Pretty simple. The board, the display with its backpack, a breadboard and four jumper wires: SCL, SDA, power and ground.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's a PlatformIO project. You clone the repo, build, and flash the ESP32. After boot, you read the device's IP address from the serial monitor and open it in a browser. The repository also has Android and firmware subprojects for a fuller setup around the same device.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's MIT licensed, and the project page links to the repository.
